A0030.title: Business-Level Honeypot
A0030.definition: A fake business resource system built specifically for attackers rather than normal users.
A0030.description: This resource system should ensure that it will not be accessed by normal users during normal business access or request processes, but can be discovered and accessed by attackers through resource ID enumeration, reverse engineering, packet capture, cracking, and other methods. Any access to the fake business resource system is therefore from an attacker. This serves two purposes: first, it immediately alerts the business that a resource has been targeted and attacked; second, it enables continuous tracking of the attacker's identity, characteristics, and behavior to facilitate countermeasure upgrades or related handling.
A0030.limitation: Completely ineffective against attack behavior that perfectly simulates normal user access.

references.title: Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS)

A0030-001.title: Dynamic Beaconing and Honeypot Traps
A0030-001.definition: Active perception sub-measures — dynamic beacons, loop traps, fake timestamps, hidden honeypot resource IDs/APIs, special-function popups, and dynamic HTTP header injection — that induce attackers to expose themselves and enable continuous tracking of their behavioral characteristics.
A0030-001.description: Dynamic beaconing and honeypot traps are the active-perception sub-measure of the business-level honeypot (A0030). Concrete forms include: dynamic beacons (hidden beacons dynamically inserted into pages that normal users would never trigger but crawlers will request — triggering marks the access as automated), loop traps (fake resources that trap crawlers in infinite loops or repeated requests, draining their resources and exposing behavior), fake timestamps/parameters (deceptive timestamps or parameters mixed into responses to induce crawlers to collect erroneous data), hidden honeypot resource IDs and honeypot API endpoints (fake resources not exposed in normal business flows, discoverable only via resource enumeration or reverse engineering), special-function popups (ads, red envelopes — visible to normal users but abnormally interacted with by crawlers, used to collect crawler interaction features), and dynamic HTTP header injection (honeypot-marker headers dynamically added to responses to track whether the crawler carries them back). The common goal: without affecting normal users, make automated visitors expose themselves proactively, so the server can continuously track the attacker's identity, characteristics, and behavior patterns — providing a basis for countermeasure upgrades and disposition.
A0030-001.limitation: Effectiveness depends on stealth — once honeypot resources or beacon logic is identified and avoided by attackers, the measure fails. Advanced attackers can filter out beacon requests via behavioral analysis and comparison with normal business flows. Improperly designed traps may affect normal users or be indexed by search engines, causing negative impact. Trap forms must be continuously updated to maintain the adversarial edge.
